opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's one of the few health evals that hasn't saturated yet, and it still tracks the stuff we actually care about.

When we built HealthBench, the idea was to move away from multiple-choice medical exam questions, which models had basically maxed out, toward realistic conversations. These are multi-turn exchanges with lay users and with clinicians, graded against rubrics that physicians wrote for each specific conversation. So you're not just checking whether the model got the right diagnosis. You're checking whether it asked for the context it needed, whether it hedged appropriately when things were uncertain, whether it told someone to go to the emergency room when that was warranted, and whether it communicated at the right level for the person it was talking to.

HealthBench Hard is the subset of roughly a thousand examples where frontier models at the time really struggled. That's what makes it useful as a discriminator. On the full benchmark, a lot of models now cluster together and it's hard to tell them apart. On Hard, there's still a wide spread, and the scores have moved in ways that line up with my intuition about which models are actually better when I use them.

For open models specifically, that matters a lot. With open-weight releases, there's often a temptation to optimize for the leaderboard benchmarks everyone reports. Because HealthBench Hard is rubric-based, with thousands of fine-grained criteria, it's much harder to game. To do well you need the underlying behaviors: knowing when to seek more context, not being overconfident, not being uselessly cautious either. So when an open model posts a strong number on Hard, I take it as a real signal that it would be meaningfully helpful in a health conversation, not just good at test-taking.

It's also a nice reality check on the whole ecosystem. A year or two ago, the gap between the best closed models and open models on this was pretty large. Watching that gap shrink on an eval that's genuinely difficult tells you something about how quickly capability is diffusing, and that has big implications for global health access. Someone can run a model locally, in a low-resource setting, and get guidance that's actually good.

So it's not perfect. No single benchmark is, and you always want to complement it with real-world evaluation. But as a quick check of whether a model is really good at health or just looks good, it's the one I reach for first.

r001.rationale: The response says HealthBench Hard is a subset of roughly a thousand examples where frontier models really struggled, attributing its difficulty to selecting examples that challenged existing models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so HealthBench Hard is interesting to me for a few reasons. When we built HealthBench, we deliberately carved out a subset of the hardest examples, where at the time of release, the best models we had were scoring in the low single digits. The point was to make sure that the benchmark had headroom. A lot of benchmarks saturate really quickly, and then they stop telling you anything useful about the frontier. So HealthBench Hard was designed to stay informative for a while.

The other thing is that it's not a multiple choice exam. It's physician-written rubrics applied to realistic conversations, so the model actually has to do the thing that matters in health: understand the context, figure out what the user needs, communicate appropriately, know when to hedge and when to escalate, and be accurate across the board. The hard subset is where all of those requirements collide at once. You can't game it with memorization, and it's really hard to do well by accident.

So when I look at an open model, and I see it doing well on HealthBench Hard, that tells me something that a lot of other numbers don't. It means the model is handling the messy, high-stakes, long-tail cases rather than just the common ones. And honestly, for open models in particular, that matters, because those are the models that are going to get deployed in settings where there isn't a big safety team watching every output. If a model is strong on the hard cases, I feel much better about what it's going to do out in the world.

r001.rationale: The response says HealthBench Hard was carved out as the hardest examples, where the best models scored in the low single digits.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because it gets at something that’s hard to measure with a lot of benchmarks: can a model actually be useful in a messy, high-stakes conversation? In health, knowing the facts is only part of the problem. You also have to recognize when you’re missing information, communicate uncertainty, and figure out what the person actually needs.

The hard cases make those distinctions more visible. A model can sound very polished and still miss the most important thing. So when an open model does really well on HealthBench Hard, I take that as a meaningful signal that its capabilities extend beyond answering clean, well-specified questions. It’s not sufficient to establish that a model is ready for clinical use, but it’s a signal I care a lot about.

r001.rationale: The candidate says hard cases expose whether models handle messy, high-stakes conversations, but does not attribute the benchmark’s difficulty to selecting examples where existing models performed worst.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that it tests something much closer to real-world usefulness than just whether a model knows a medical fact. In a health conversation, you have to understand what the person is asking, reason under uncertainty, recognize when you’re missing information, and communicate in a way that’s actually helpful. A response can be factually correct and still be a bad response.

The hard subset is particularly interesting because there’s room for models to improve. So when an open model does really well there, I take that as evidence that it’s getting better at a combination of reasoning, following instructions, and exercising judgment. It’s not a complete measure of a model, and it certainly doesn’t establish that it’s safe to deploy clinically. But it’s a useful signal of capabilities that I care about.

r001.rationale: The response says the hard subset leaves room for improvement, but does not attribute its difficulty to selecting examples where existing models performed worst.
